analysis.one_liner: Requires ticket sellers and resale sites to disclose hidden fees, held-back tickets, and face values.
analysis.headline: With one sponsor and three cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules for how concert and sports tickets are sold and resold. Primary sellers would have to disclose how many tickets they hold back from the public, show all fees in the advertised price, refund those fees, and stop forcing buyers to resell only through the seller's own exchange. Resale sites would have to show each ticket's face value and true seat location, admit when they don't actually hold the ticket, and face a ban on software that buys up tickets faster than fans can. Enforcement would come through the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Fans buying tickets to concerts, sports, and theater. They would see the total price with fees up front, learn how many tickets were withheld from public sale and where those went, know the face value and exact seat of any resale ticket, and get refunds when a resale site sells a ticket it doesn't have.

how_it_helps.text: Primary sellers must disclose at least seven days before a sale how many tickets they are offering and how many are withheld from the general public, ending the practice of quietly setting aside most seats for insiders.
Advertised prices must include all ancillary charges such as service, convenience, and parking fees, and refunds must return those fees, so the sticker price matches what buyers actually pay.
Primary sellers can no longer require that consumers resell tickets only through a channel the seller chooses, freeing fans to resell where they like.

Resale sites must show each ticket's face value and precise seat location, admit when they do not possess the ticket at time of sale, and explain refund procedures if the ticket doesn't match its description.
Software that circumvents a ticketing website's security measures to buy tickets ahead of ordinary fans would be banned, along with knowingly reselling tickets obtained that way.
Enforcement combines FTC rules, state attorney general lawsuits, and a private right of action with $1,000 damages per violated requirement plus attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Primary ticket sellers, venues, and resale marketplaces would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from undisclosed fees, restricted-resale requirements, and insider allocations; these costs could partly be passed to fans through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ticketing platforms, resale sites, and venues

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on disclosure rather than price limits, so a sold-out show can still resell far above face value; it reveals insider allocations but does not forbid them.

The private right of action awards $1,000 per violated requirement per ticket plus attorney fees, which could expose even small venues and sellers to costly litigation over technical disclosure slips.

Rules apply to every primary seller, including small venues and local promoters, whose compliance costs would likely flow into ticket prices; and mandatory all-in price displays can make advertised tickets look costlier to casual buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core wins are real but modest: fans learn what a ticket truly costs, what they are buying on resale, and how many seats never reached public sale. The bill would not cap prices or guarantee access, and its litigation penalty and compliance costs are the honest costs of enforcement. On balance it is a consumer-transparency bill, and its main weakness is that it died without any debate or amendment process that could have refined it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended; no markup, vote, or floor action ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Pascrell Jr. introduced the bill on May 16, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Four days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, which took no further action.
The bill attracted three cosponsors, all House Democrats, and never advanced out of committee before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Primary ticketing platforms, resale marketplaces, and professional brokers are better off because the bill died: none of its disclosure, fee-refund, or anti-bot requirements took effect, and fans continued paying opaque fees and competing against automated buyers without federal protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ticketing platforms, resale sites, and brokers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the bill's sponsor and all three cosponsors were House Democrats, while the committee where it stalled was controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Primary ticket sellers and ticketing platforms
industries.note: These companies profit from undisclosed service and convenience fees, from withholding large blocks of tickets for presales and insiders, and from forcing resales through their own exchange. The bill would require all-in pricing, fee refunds, disclosure of withheld tickets, and an end to exclusive-resale requirements.

Resale sites would have to show face value and true seat location, disclose when they don't hold the ticket, and stop selling bot-acquired tickets. Producers and brokers make money on the spread between face value and resale price, which disclosure narrows.
They gain from bans on bot circumvention and fake affiliation claims, but lose the ability to restrict resale to their own channels, a tool some performers used to fight scalping.
Their entire business depends on circumventing ticketing websites to buy inventory ahead of fans; the bill bans that software and the resale of tickets obtained with it.
